### Observed differences

- In the later window, A30, A31 and A36 still appear in every trace, but each occurs only about once per trace instead of about 3.4 times; the share of traces in which an activity repeats itself fell from about 75 in 100 to about 1–2 in 100. [OCC001, OCC002, OCC003]
- In the later window, only about 4 in 100 of A36's outgoing transitions go to A30 (about 70 in 100 before), while about 93 in 100 go to A25 (about 29 in 100 before). [DIR003]
- The dominant successor links held: in the later window A30 still leads to A31 in about 97 in 100 of its outgoing transitions (about 99 before), and A31 still leads to A36 in about 98 in 100 (about 99 before), with only minor redistribution among rare edges. [DIR001, DIR002]
- In the later window, the A30–A36 pair became strictly ordered: the two activities co-occur in all traces in both windows, but A30 precedes A36 in about 98 in 100 traces (about 25 before), with interleaved-or-repeated orderings dropping from about 75 in 100 to about 2 in 100. [REL001]
- In the later window, occurrence positions became more deterministic: A30's mean relative position moved slightly earlier (about 0.44 to 0.42) and its spread roughly halved (about 0.12 to 0.07); A36's mean stayed near 0.49 while its spread roughly halved (about 0.12 to 0.06). [POS001, POS002]
- In the later window, A36 follows A30 at an event distance of 2 in about 89 in 100 of observed pairs, whereas before, the distances were more dispersed with a visible share at distance 5; repeated A30–A30 and A36–A36 pairs and A36-followed-by-A30 pairs nearly disappeared, though those after-window figures rest on only 1–2 observations each. [LAG001, LAG002, LAG003, LAG004]

### Inference

Support level: Supported hypothesis

The evidence supports the possibility that the repeated cycling through A30, A31 and A36 was largely discontinued: in the later window each of the three activities runs essentially once per trace in the fixed order A30 → A31 → A36, and A36 then continues to A25 rather than returning to A30, whereas before, all three activities recurred in about three quarters of traces and A36 sent about 70 in 100 of its outgoing transitions back to A30. [OCC001, OCC002, OCC003, DIR003, REL001, LAG002, LAG003]

Supporting signs: 13 items qualified against roughly 0.5 expected if nothing had changed, so the set as a whole is unlikely under random re-splitting; the repetition drop, the routing change at A36, the fixed ordering and the distance-2 gap all describe one coherent underlying difference rather than independent confirmations; the outgoing-transition counts behind the routing profiles (about 690 before versus about 210 after) match the fall in occurrences per trace; and every difference is larger than in about 995 of 1000 random re-splits. [OCC001, OCC002, OCC003, DIR001, DIR002, DIR003, REL001, LAG001, LAG002, LAG003, LAG004]

Limitations: the two windows are finite samples, so a shift in the mix of trace variants — a repeating variant frequent in the earlier window and rare in the later one without any structural modification — cannot be ruled out; the near-disappearance of repeated pairs rests on only 1–2 after-window observations, and low recurrence shows only that repetition was rarely observed in the later window, not that it is absent from the process. [LAG001, LAG003, LAG004]
